note: The repo's claim catalog. Every entry binds a domain claim to the machine result that is supposed to support it. scripts/check-claims.sh is the oracle: it runs each check and decides whether the repo still says what the book says it says. See claims/README.md.

claims.domain_claim: a refund is only ever recorded for an order that is in the refunded state, and every payment attempt resolves
claims.unguarded_reason: no breaking variant yet: the probe predates the dual-check convention and the interesting negative is a fairness change, not a constant flip
claims.domain_wording: the async checkout workflow cannot leave money refunded against a non-refunded order, and no payment attempt hangs forever

claims.domain_claim: replaying the event log is deterministic, snapshots are prefixes of it, and the balance never goes negative
claims.unguarded_reason: no breaking variant yet; the four invariants each want their own negative and none has been written
claims.domain_wording: rebuilding the ledger from its events gives the same balance every time, and a snapshot never disagrees with the log it came from

claims.domain_claim: mailboxes stay bounded, per-pair message order is preserved, and every sent message is eventually delivered
claims.unguarded_reason: no breaking variant yet: the bound and the FIFO discipline are structural in the model rather than selected by a constant
claims.domain_wording: no actor's queue grows without bound, two messages between the same pair never overtake each other, and nothing is dropped

claims.domain_claim: an accepted game tick carries a self-checking transcript, and a dispute always carries sound evidence
claims.unguarded_reason: no breaking variant yet; the negatives worth writing are per-invariant cheats and none has been modelled
claims.domain_wording: a peer cannot get a tick accepted without having committed before revealing, and a dispute cannot be raised without the evidence to back it

claims.domain_claim: traffic only ever reaches a healthy target, new traffic waits for the database, and a ready rollout finishes
claims.unguarded_reason: no breaking variant yet: the obvious negative (cut over before the migration lands) is not yet expressed as a constant
claims.domain_wording: a blue/green cutover never sends users to an unhealthy target group, and never shifts traffic before the schema is ready

claims.domain_claim: at most Cap events are granted, under every interleaving of concurrent workers
claims.domain_wording: an atomic check-and-increment holds the limit no matter how the two workers interleave

claims.domain_claim: splitting the read from the record lets two workers both pass the check and over-grant
claims.domain_wording: two requests arriving together each read the old count and each grant, so the cap is exceeded by one

claims.domain_claim: an at-least-once retried request causes at most one external charge, and every request eventually settles
claims.domain_wording: reserve the key first, resume a half-written row on retry, and let the provider dedupe: at most one charge, and nothing wedges

claims.domain_claim: writing the key row after the provider call lets a crash in that window charge the customer twice
claims.domain_wording: the process dies between charging and storing the key, the client retries, and the customer is charged a second time

claims.domain_claim: reserve-first with a hard 409 on a reserved key never double charges, and wedges the key forever after one crash
claims.domain_wording: safety holds and liveness does not: the key is stuck at reserved and every retry gets a 409, so the payment never completes and no alarm fires

claims.domain_claim: committed member rows never exceed the plan's seat limit
claims.source_of_truth: the invite handler's SQL and the isolation level the pool actually sets
claims.domain_wording: under PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE the second transaction aborts at commit and the limit holds

claims.domain_claim: committed member rows never exceed the plan's seat limit — held by an explicit row lock instead of the isolation level
claims.source_of_truth: the invite handler's SQL and the isolation level the pool actually sets
claims.domain_wording: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the org row materialises the conflict the two inserts do not have, so snapshot isolation is enough

claims.domain_claim: plain snapshot isolation admits the write skew and the seat limit breaks
claims.domain_wording: two admins clicking Invite within the same second both see one free seat, and the org ends up with two members on a one-seat plan

claims.domain_claim: a quiet day's production log is a behaviour the model admits at the isolation level we claim, and the limit held
claims.source_of_truth: the postgres statement log joined to the app request log
claims.domain_wording: nothing contended and nobody went over: what a conformance check says on almost every day it runs

claims.domain_claim: a log that contended and lost to a 40001 is admitted only by SERIALIZABLE, so it is positive evidence for the isolation level
claims.source_of_truth: the postgres statement log joined to the app request log
claims.domain_wording: the pool really is on SSI: the overlapping invite was rolled back with a serialization failure rather than committed

claims.domain_claim: the incident log is not a behaviour the model admits at the isolation level ops claim the pool is set to
claims.source_of_truth: the postgres statement log joined to the app request log
claims.domain_wording: log line 6 is the second COMMIT, which SSI would have aborted: this history cannot have happened under SERIALIZABLE

claims.domain_claim: at the isolation level that does admit the incident log, the seat limit really was exceeded
claims.source_of_truth: the postgres statement log joined to the app request log
claims.domain_wording: the pool was on REPEATABLE READ and the org finished with two members on a one-seat plan
